chunks.title: Conjunctival naevus & papilloma
chunks.tldr: Naevus: commonest pigmented lesion, juxtalimbal, mobile, contains cysts (>50%), appears in 1st–2nd decade; malignant change <1%. Worry if: palpebral/fornix site, feeder vessels, sudden growth, new after age 20. Papilloma: HPV 6/11, sessile or frond-like.
points: Naevus types: compound (commonest), subepithelial, junctional.
Often amelanotic; can get inflamed in teens (mimics malignancy).
Papilloma: limbus, fornix, caruncle; may regress.
Papilloma Rx: excision + cryo to base; recurrences → interferon, MMC, CO2 laser, oral cimetidine.
chunks.hook: Cysts = calm (naevus). Fornix pigment = fear.

cards.q: Key clinical feature favouring conjunctival naevus over melanoma?
cards.a: Intralesional cysts (and mobility, onset in childhood, juxtalimbal location).

cards.q: HPV types in conjunctival papilloma?

chunks.title: Dermoid, dermolipoma, granuloma & melanosis
chunks.tldr: Limbal dermoid (choristoma): inferotemporal limbus, hairs → Goldenhar. Dermolipoma: adults, superotemporal, don't operate deep (ptosis, dry eye, motility). Pyogenic granuloma: after chalazion/squint surgery → topical steroid. Benign melanosis: bilateral, dark skin, flat, mobile.
points: Dermoid treat for astigmatism/amblyopia, dellen, cosmesis (lamellar keratosclerectomy if big).
Goldenhar: malar/mandible hypoplasia, ear tags, hemivertebrae, lid coloboma.
Also: Treacher Collins, linear naevus sebaceous of Jadassohn.
Dermolipoma vs prolapsed orbital fat vs lacrimal gland lobe vs lymphoma.
Pyogenic granuloma = neither pyogenic nor granulomatous.
Others: epibulbar telangiectasia (Sturge–Weber), pseudo-epitheliomatous hyperplasia, melanocytoma, post-radiation angioma.
chunks.hook: Goldenhar = Golden (yellow) limbal lump + ear tags.

cards.q: Syndrome associated with limbal dermoid?
First-line treatment for pyogenic granuloma?

chunks.title: PAM / C-MIN
chunks.tldr: Unilateral, flat golden–brown patches in a middle-aged white person (median 56). Without atypia: harmless. With severe atypia = melanoma in situ. ~75% of conjunctival melanomas arise from PAM. Evert lids. Rx: excision ± cryo, MMC.
points: C-MIN graded 0–10 (5 = melanoma in situ).
Bigger extent (clock hours) = higher risk.
DDx: naevus, benign melanosis, ocular melanocytosis, Addison, pigmented SCC.
Observe <1 clock hour (photos) or excise.
MMC 0.04% QDS 1 week cycles with punctal plugs; corneal part: alcohol epitheliectomy + MMC.
Lifelong follow-up.
chunks.hook: Benign melanosis = Both eyes, Black patients. PAM = one eye, Pale patients.

cards.q: Which PAM is a melanoma precursor?
Proportion of conjunctival melanomas arising from PAM?

chunks.title: Conjunctival melanoma
chunks.tldr: ~2% of ocular cancers; from PAM (75%), naevus (25%). Black/grey vascular nodule, may be fixed. Bad sites: caruncle, fornix, lid margin; thickness ≥2 mm. Mortality ~30% at 10 yrs; spreads to lymph nodes. Rx: wide no-touch excision + cryo/MMC/radiotherapy.
points: Use fresh instruments to close (avoid seeding).
Screen: nodes, LFTs, liver US, chest X-ray, PET/CT; sentinel node biopsy.
Exenteration doesn't improve survival — only for extensive disease.
BRAF V600E in ~50% → vemurafenib for metastases.
chunks.hook: Conjunctival melanoma goes to the Nodes (like skin); uveal goes to the Liver.

cards.q: Poor-prognosis locations for conjunctival melanoma?
Targeted therapy for metastatic conjunctival melanoma?
cards.a: BRAF inhibitor (vemurafenib) if BRAF V600E present.

chunks.title: OSSN (squamous neoplasia)
chunks.tldr: Spectrum: dysplasia → CIS → invasive SCC. Interpalpebral limbus; gelatinous, leukoplakic, papillomatous, feeder vessels. Risks: UV, HIV, HPV16, ciclosporin, smoking, xeroderma pigmentosum. Rx: excision 2–4 mm + cryo or topical interferon α-2b (~80% resolve), MMC, 5-FU.
points: Young patient with OSSN → test for HIV (Africa: women + HIV).
AS-OCT/UBM for depth; impression cytology.
Don't cut below Bowman's layer.
Recurrence 5–33% after excision.
Immunosuppressed: lifelong daily interferon drops.
chunks.hook: Sun + HIV + HPV = OSSN.

cards.q: Topical agent achieving ~80% resolution of OSSN with few side effects?
Systemic disease to test for in young patients with OSSN?

chunks.title: Lymphoma, amyloid & Kaposi
chunks.tldr: Lymphoma: salmon-pink mobile fornix patch; mostly MALT B-cell; 30% systemic → biopsy + staging; radiotherapy. Amyloid: light chains, Congo red apple-green, mostly local. Kaposi: purple nodule in AIDS (HHV-8).
points: Biopsy other inferior fornix too.
Bilateral → systemic more likely.
Lymphoma Rx: EBRT, rituximab, interferon, chemo.
Mantle cell lymphoma: poor survival.
Kaposi: optimise HAART, local radiotherapy/excision.
chunks.hook: Salmon patch = lymphoma.

cards.q: Typical appearance of conjunctival lymphoma?
cards.a: Salmon-pink, mobile subconjunctival infiltrate, often in the fornix.

chunks.title: Iris naevus, freckles & melanoma
chunks.tldr: Iris naevus: up to 8% transform over 15 yrs — risk: age <40, inferior, bleeding, diffuse, feathery margin, ectropion uveae. Iris melanoma (8% of uveal): inferior, ≥3 mm × 1 mm, vessels, good prognosis (5% mets at 10 yrs). Rx: iridectomy/iridocyclectomy, plaque, proton.
points: Uveal melanoma risks: fair skin, light iris, dysplastic naevi, naevus of Ota/ocular melanocytosis, welding.
Iris melanoma presents a decade earlier than choroidal.
Signs: pupil distortion, ectropion uveae, hyphaema, glaucoma.
UBM to exclude ciliary body spread.
Freckle: flat, normal cell number.
Brushfield spots: Down syndrome. Lisch nodules: NF1.
Iris mets: fast, white/pink, uveitis, hyphaema (breast, lung, skin melanoma).
JXG: toddlers, yellow iris lesion, spontaneous hyphaema, skin nodules.
chunks.hook: Iris melanoma = Inferior, Infrequently fatal.

cards.q: Cause of spontaneous hyphaema in a toddler with skin nodules?
Metastatic rate of iris melanoma at 10 years?

chunks.title: Iris cysts
chunks.tldr: Pigment epithelial cysts: peripheral bulge, harmless (DDx ciliary body melanoma → UBM/AS-OCT). Stromal: translucent; congenital ones aggressive. Traumatic/implantation cysts grow → glaucoma. Miotic cysts: pupil margin; prevent with phenylephrine.
points: Epithelial cysts may float free.
Stromal cyst Rx: aspiration, excision, ethanol sclerosis.
Implantation cysts after penetrating injury/surgery.
Parasitic: very rare.
chunks.hook: Bump behind the iris? UBM it.

cards.q: How are miotic-induced iris cysts prevented?

chunks.title: Ciliary body melanoma & medulloepithelioma
chunks.tldr: ~12% of uveal melanomas; hidden → sentinel episcleral vessel, lens displacement (astigmatism, cataract), angle invasion. Ix: UBM, gonioscopy, biopsy. Rx: iridocyclectomy, plaque/proton, enucleation. Medulloepithelioma: child, ciliary body mass, leukocoria.
points: DDx: iridociliary cyst, uveal effusion.
May erode iris root or exit through sclera.
Check liver.
Medulloepithelioma (diktyoma): from inner optic cup; may need enucleation.
chunks.hook: One fat episcleral vessel = look behind the iris.

cards.q: Subtle external sign of ciliary body melanoma?

chunks.title: Choroidal naevus & red flags
chunks.tldr: 5–10% of whites; grey, feathery, drusen + halo. Growth in adult = suspicious. Risk factors 'TFSOM-UHHD': Thickness >2 mm, Fluid, Symptoms, Orange pigment, Margin ≤3 mm disc, Ultrasound Hollow, Halo absent, Drusen absent.
points: Lifetime transformation up to 1%.
FAF shows orange pigment (bright); OCT finds subtle SRF; US measures thickness/hollowness.
FA doesn't distinguish naevus from melanoma.
Review: none suspicious → 6 m then yearly; 1–2 → 4–6 monthly; ≥3 → ocular oncology.
Long stability doesn't guarantee safety.
chunks.hook: 'To Find Small Ocular Melanoma Using Helpful Hints Daily'.

cards.q: Name four risk factors for a choroidal naevus becoming melanoma.
cards.a: Thickness >2 mm, subretinal fluid, symptoms, orange pigment (also margin near disc, acoustic hollowness, no halo, no drusen).

cards.q: Which overlying features favour a benign choroidal naevus?

chunks.title: Choroidal melanoma: features & tests
chunks.tldr: Commonest adult primary intraocular cancer (80% of uveal). Grey-brown dome, orange pigment, SRF, collar-stud (mushroom) if through Bruch. US: low–medium internal reflectivity, acoustic hollowing, choroidal excavation. Mets → liver; ~50% mortality at 10 yrs. BAP1/monosomy 3 = bad.
points: Spindle cells (better) vs epithelioid (worse).
~60% within 3 mm of disc/fovea.
Other signs: sentinel vessels, folds, rubeosis, glaucoma, cataract.
FA: dual circulation, late leak (not diagnostic). ICGA: hypo. FAF: diffuse bright.
MRI: melanin is T1 bright, T2 dark; extraocular spread.
Biopsy (FNA or 25G vitrectomy) + genetic profiling for prognosis.
Only 1–2% have mets at diagnosis; LFTs + liver US mainstay.
chunks.hook: Mushroom on ultrasound = melanoma.

cards.q: Pathognomonic B-scan shape of choroidal melanoma?
Typical internal reflectivity of melanoma on A/B-scan?
cards.a: Low to medium, with acoustic hollowing.

chunks.title: Choroidal melanoma: mimics
chunks.tldr: Pigmented mimics: naevus, melanocytoma (black, disc), CHRPE (flat, lacunae), haemorrhage (CNV, macroaneurysm, PEHCR), metastatic skin melanoma. Non-pigmented: haemangioma (orange), metastasis (cream, multiple), granuloma, posterior scleritis (pain), peripheral CNV, vortex ampulla (disappears with pressure).
points: Haemangioma: smooth orange dome, high internal reflectivity.
Metastasis: big exudative RD, history of cancer.
Vortex vein ampulla: small, brown, near equator.
chunks.hook: Orange = haemangioma; cream = metastasis; brown = melanoma.

cards.q: Non-pigmented choroidal mass with pain – consider?

chunks.title: Choroidal melanoma: treatment
chunks.tldr: Plaque brachytherapy: <20 mm base, ≤10 mm thick; survival = enucleation (COMS). Proton beam: large/posterior. TTT, trans-scleral resection for selected. Enucleation: large, disc invasion, blind eye. Check the correct eye with ophthalmoscopy after draping.
points: Plaque regression starts 1–2 months; complications: cataract, radiation retinopathy/papillopathy, toxic tumour syndrome (anti-VEGF/steroid/endoresection).
Proton: tantalum markers; lash loss, keratitis.
Stereotactic radiotherapy: higher complication rate.
TTT: small tumours or adjunct; recurrences common.
AU-011 light-activated particles: trial for small tumours.
No proven benefit of systemic chemo without mets.
chunks.hook: Plaque = Preserve eye, same survival.

cards.q: Size limits for plaque brachytherapy?
cards.a: Basal diameter <20 mm and thickness ≤10 mm.

cards.q: Essential safety step before enucleation?
cards.a: Ophthalmoscopy after draping to confirm the tumour eye.

chunks.title: Choroidal haemangiomas & melanocytoma
chunks.tldr: Circumscribed: orange posterior dome, no systemic link, exudative RD in young adults; ICGA early bright, late washout; US high reflectivity. Rx: PDT. Diffuse: 'tomato ketchup' fundus in Sturge–Weber. Melanocytoma: jet-black disc lesion, darker skin, benign, may have RAPD.
points: Circumscribed: median 6 mm × 3 mm; FA early spotty, late intense.
Other Rx: TTT, laser, radiotherapy, anti-VEGF, oral propranolol (for fluid).
Diffuse: risk exudative RD → neovascular glaucoma; PDT/low-dose radiotherapy.
Melanocytoma: women, ~50 yrs; FA hypo; rare malignant change.
chunks.hook: Sturge–Weber: port-wine face, ketchup fundus, glaucoma.

cards.q: Treatment of choice for symptomatic circumscribed choroidal haemangioma?
Diffuse choroidal haemangioma is associated with?

chunks.title: Choroidal osteoma & metastases
chunks.tldr: Osteoma: young women, orange→yellow-white plaque near disc, scalloped edges; US/CT: bone-bright + shadowing; CNV risk. Metastasis: commonest uveal tumour (choroid 90%); breast (known history) and lung (may be first sign); creamy, flat, multifocal, bilateral, big exudative RD; median survival 8–12 months.
points: Osteoma: bilateral 10–20%; EDI-OCT lattice like cancellous bone; poor VA if fovea involved.
DDx: sclerochoroidal calcification (older, bilateral, yellow-white).
Mets: no dual circulation on FA; ICGA finds extra deposits.
Find primary: breast exam/mammogram, chest imaging, LFTs, PET/CT.
Rx: systemic chemo, radiotherapy (EBRT/plaque), PDT/TTT, anti-VEGF.
chunks.hook: Bone in the eye of a young woman = osteoma. Cream patches in an older woman = breast mets.

cards.q: Commonest primaries for choroidal metastasis?
Imaging hallmark of choroidal osteoma?
cards.a: Highly reflective plaque with orbital shadowing on US; bone density on CT.

chunks.title: Retinoblastoma: genetics
chunks.tldr: Commonest childhood eye cancer (~1:18,000). RB1 (13q14), Knudson two-hit. Heritable 40%: bilateral/multifocal, younger, pinealoblastoma (trilateral), later osteosarcoma, sarcomas, melanoma. Non-heritable 60%: unilateral (90% of unilateral cases).
points: Germline AD; ~40% of offspring affected (incomplete penetrance).
Sibling risk: 2% if parents healthy, 40% if parent affected; sporadic unilateral → ~1%.
Second cancer risk ~6% → ×5 with external beam radiotherapy.
Screen at-risk siblings: prenatal US, exam soon after birth, regularly till 4–5 yrs.
Examine parents for retinomas/scars.
Histology: small blue cells, Flexner–Wintersteiner & Homer–Wright rosettes, fleurettes.
chunks.hook: RB = Really Bad if Both eyes (germline → more cancers).

cards.q: What is trilateral retinoblastoma?
Why avoid external beam radiotherapy in heritable RB?
cards.a: Greatly increases second malignancies (e.g. sarcoma) in the field.

chunks.title: Retinoblastoma: presentation & groups
chunks.tldr: Age: bilateral <1 yr, unilateral ~2 yrs. Leukocoria 60%, squint 20% (→ dilated fundus in every child with squint). White dome with calcification; endophytic (seeds) vs exophytic (RD). EUA, US/MRI (CT radiation). Groups A–E.
points: Others: red painful eye/glaucoma, buphthalmos, pseudo-uveitis, orbital cellulitis mimic, proptosis.
Red reflex test screens.
EUA: IOP, corneal diameter, AC, drawings/photos, refraction.
MRI: optic nerve, extraocular, pineal.
Spread: optic nerve → CSF → brain; nodes, lung, bone.
A: <3 mm away from fovea/disc. B: >3 mm or macular/juxtapapillary/SRF. C: focal seeds ≤3 mm. D: diffuse seeds. E: >50% globe, NVG, AC/optic nerve.
chunks.hook: White pupil in a photo = RB until proven otherwise.

cards.q: Most common presentation of retinoblastoma?
Which imaging detects calcification without radiation?
cards.a: Ultrasound (CT also does but with radiation; MRI does not).

chunks.title: Retinoblastoma: treatment
chunks.tldr: Chemoreduction (IV carboplatin, etoposide, vincristine) + focal TTT/cryo; intra-arterial melphalan (great for group D); intravitreal melphalan for seeds; plaque. Enucleation for group E, NVG, AC/optic nerve invasion — with ≥10 mm optic nerve. Survival >95% in good centres.
points: Cryo: triple freeze–thaw for anterior tumours.
EBRT only for relapse after chemo; side effects: cataract, retinopathy, orbital hypoplasia.
Adjuvant chemo if retrolaminar optic nerve or massive choroidal invasion.
EBRT if tumour at cut nerve end or through sclera.
Frequent follow-up for new tumours (heritable).
chunks.hook: Take 10 mm of nerve with the eye.

cards.q: Minimum optic nerve length at enucleation for RB?
Treatment offering high globe salvage in group D RB?

chunks.title: Leukocoria differentials
chunks.tldr: PFV (microphthalmic, retrolental mass, elongated ciliary processes), Coats (boys, unilateral, older, exudate), ROP, Toxocara, uveitis, vitreoretinal dysplasia (Norrie, incontinentia pigmenti, Walker–Warburg), retinoma, astrocytoma, cataract.
points: Anterior PFV: lens opacity, angle closure; early surgery may help.
Posterior PFV: fold from disc to ora; untreatable.
Norrie (XLR, NDP): blind boys, deaf, learning disability.
Incontinentia pigmenti (XLD, NEMO): girls; blistering → swirled pigment; teeth, hair, CNS.
Walker–Warburg (AR): lissencephaly, Peters, microphthalmos.
Retinoma: benign RB variant, calcified scar; rare transformation.
chunks.hook: Small eye + stretched ciliary processes = PFV, not RB.

cards.q: Key sign of persistent fetal vasculature?
cards.a: Retrolental fibrovascular mass with elongated ciliary processes in a microphthalmic eye.

cards.q: X-linked leukocoria with deafness in boys?

chunks.title: Astrocytoma & tuberous sclerosis
chunks.tldr: Retinal astrocytic hamartoma: white/yellow, mulberry calcified nodule; ~50% of tuberous sclerosis. TS (AD): epilepsy, learning difficulty, adenoma sebaceum, ash-leaf spots (Wood lamp), shagreen patch, subungual fibromas, renal angiomyolipoma, cardiac rhabdomyoma.
points: Also in NF1, RP.
Most need no treatment.
OCT: granular hyper-reflective inner retina; FA: superficial vessels, late leak.
TS: 60% sporadic; subependymal nodules, giant cell astrocytoma.
Iris hypopigmentation, atypical colobomas.
chunks.hook: Mulberry in the retina + ash leaf on the skin = tuberous sclerosis.

cards.q: Classic triad of tuberous sclerosis?

chunks.title: Capillary haemangioma & VHL
chunks.tldr: Orange-red ball with dilated feeder artery + draining vein; peripheral or juxtapapillary. Multiple = von Hippel–Lindau (chr 3, AD): cerebellar haemangioblastoma, renal cell carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, pancreatic tumours, cysts. Rx: laser (small), cryo (larger), PDT/anti-VEGF for disc lesions.
points: VHL patients present younger (median 18 vs 31).
Complications: exudate, ERM, TRD/RRD, VH, glaucoma.
Observe asymptomatic juxtapapillary lesions.
Cryo may cause temporary exudative RD.
Screening: retina from 2–5 yrs; urine catecholamines; renal US from 15; brain/abdo MRI 2-yearly; audiometry if symptoms; genetic testing for relatives.
chunks.hook: VHL = Very Hard on Lots of organs (brain, kidney, adrenal, eye).

cards.q: Chromosome and gene in von Hippel–Lindau?
cards.a: VHL tumour suppressor gene on chromosome 3.

cards.q: Treatment for a small peripheral retinal capillary haemangioma?

chunks.title: Cavernous, racemose & vasoproliferative tumours
chunks.tldr: Cavernous: 'bunch of grapes' with fluid levels (sedimented RBCs), no leak, don't laser; skin/CNS cavernomas. Racemose (AV communication): groups 1–3; severe → Wyburn-Mason (brain AVM). Vasoproliferative: inferotemporal yellow-red mass, exudate; primary or secondary (uveitis, RP).
points: Cavernous FA: slow venous filling, plasma–RBC menisci.
Racemose: group 1 capillary plexus + macrovessel; group 2 direct; group 3 large tortuous.
Vasoproliferative Rx: cryo or plaque.
chunks.hook: Grapes with fluid levels = cavernous. Big tangled vessels + brain AVM = Wyburn-Mason.

cards.q: Why shouldn't cavernous haemangioma be lasered?
cards.a: May precipitate haemorrhage and enlargement; it rarely needs treatment.

cards.q: Retinal racemose haemangioma with ipsilateral brain AVM?

chunks.title: Primary vitreoretinal lymphoma
chunks.tldr: Older adult, 'uveitis' with vitritis + creamy sub-RPE infiltrates, no CMO, poor steroid response. Large B-cell PCNSL subset → most get brain involvement (~29 months). FA: leopard spots. Dx: vitreous biopsy (cytology, IL-10:IL-6, MYD88), MRI brain, LP. Rx: intravitreal methotrexate/rituximab, systemic chemo, radiotherapy.
points: ~20% of PCNSL have eye disease.
Hodgkin: uveitis-like; non-Hodgkin: conjunctiva/orbit.
Neurological: headache, personality change, seizures, palsies.
Vitreous cells fragile → handle sample fast.
Absence of CMO is a big clue (real uveitis almost always has CMO).
chunks.hook: Old 'uveitis' without CMO that ignores steroids = lymphoma.

cards.q: Clinical clue that vitritis may be lymphoma rather than uveitis?
cards.a: Absence of cystoid macular oedema (and poor steroid response, sub-RPE infiltrates).

cards.q: Local treatment for intraocular lymphoma?

chunks.title: CHRPE & FAP
chunks.tldr: Solitary CHRPE: flat jet-black, sharp edge, halo + lacunae; no bowel risk; rare adenoma. Grouped ('bear tracks'): one eye, sectoral, harmless. Atypical (bilateral, multiple, fishtail/comma shapes with pale edges) = FAP (APC) → colonoscopy; Gardner, Turcot.
points: 70–80% of FAP have atypical CHRPE (present at birth).
FAP untreated → colorectal cancer by 50.
Gardner: + osteomas, epidermoid cysts, fibromas.
Turcot: + brain tumours (medulloblastoma, glioma).
Solitary CHRPE slowly enlarges; review long-term.
chunks.hook: Bear tracks = fine. Fishtails in both eyes = check the colon.

cards.q: Which CHRPE pattern is associated with FAP?
cards.a: Atypical: bilateral, multiple, oval/fishtail-shaped lesions with depigmented margins.

cards.q: Gene in familial adenomatous polyposis?

chunks.title: Combined hamartoma & other RPE lesions
chunks.tldr: Combined hamartoma of retina + RPE: grey juxtapapillary lesion with ERM, retinal wrinkling, tortuous vessels; child with poor VA/squint; association NF2. Simple RPE hamartoma: tiny jet-black nodule next to the fovea. RPE adenoma: peripheral, feeder vessels, no metastasis.
points: Combined hamartoma: VA ≤6/60 in 40–50%; amblyopia therapy; vitrectomy for ERM sometimes.
RPE hyperplasia can mimic melanoma.
chunks.hook: Wrinkled grey patch by the disc in a child → combined hamartoma (think NF2).

cards.q: Systemic association of combined hamartoma of retina and RPE?

chunks.title: Paraneoplastic: BDUMP, CAR, MAR
chunks.tldr: BDUMP: bilateral multiple naevus-like lesions + fast cataract + exudative RD → hidden cancer. CAR: small cell lung ca; vision loss before cancer diagnosis; photoreceptors → ERG photopic + scotopic both down. MAR: after skin melanoma; bipolar cells → negative ERG (b-wave lost, a-wave OK); milder.
points: CAR: photopsia, glare, colour loss, night blindness, ring scotoma; fundus initially normal.
CAR without cancer = autoimmune retinopathy.
MAR: may have vitiligo; prognosis better.
BDUMP: plasmapheresis; treat primary.
chunks.hook: CAR comes before the Cancer; MAR comes after Melanoma (and flattens the b-wave).

cards.q: ERG pattern in melanoma-associated retinopathy?
cards.a: Electronegative: reduced b-wave with preserved a-wave (bipolar cell dysfunction).

cards.q: Most common cancer associated with CAR?
cards.a: Small cell carcinoma of the lung.
